title: SOLOMON HAD 700 WIVES. BUT HIS HEART WAS ALREADY BREAKING GOD’S LAW BEFORE IT TURNED AWAY.
paragraphs: SOLOMON HAD 700 WIVES. BUT HIS HEART WAS ALREADY BREAKING GOD’S LAW BEFORE IT TURNED AWAY.

The terrifying truth hidden between Deuteronomy 17 and 1 Kings 11: How the wisest king in Israel crossed a boundary God had already drawn—and why his downfall may expose the compromise we keep defending in our own lives.
The most frightening thing about Solomon’s 700 wives is not that they eventually turned his heart away from God.
It is that God had already warned Israel’s kings not to multiply wives long before Solomon ever sat on the throne.
Read that again.
Before the foreign altars. Before the incense rose to false gods. Before the kingdom began moving toward division. Before the man who prayed for wisdom became the king whose choices contradicted it.
There was already a command.
And Solomon, of all people, should have known it.
Imagine standing in Jerusalem during the height of his reign.

Gold everywhere. A magnificent temple. Foreign dignitaries arriving with gifts. Servants moving through royal corridors. A throne that commanded attention. A kingdom whose prosperity made neighboring nations marvel.
And somewhere inside that palace was a man who could explain righteousness more beautifully than almost anyone alive.
A man who understood the fear of the Lord.
A man who had heard God speak.
A man who built a house for God's name.
Yet behind the splendor, something was happening that no amount of gold could conceal.
The king was accumulating what God had forbidden kings to multiply.
And the tragedy was not waiting for him at the end of his life.
The tragedy was already growing inside his obedience.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual collapse does not begin when someone stops believing in God.
It begins when someone still believes in God but starts making exceptions to His Word.
And that is where Solomon's story becomes painfully personal.
Long before Solomon's reign, Moses gave Israel instructions concerning the kings who would one day rule over them.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.” (KJV)
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Velo yarbeh-lo nashim, velo yasur levavo.
The phrase means, in context, “And he shall not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn aside.”
Notice those words.
לֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים — lo yarbeh-lo nashim.
He shall not multiply wives for himself.
The Hebrew verb yarbeh, from the root ravah (רבה), carries the idea of increasing or multiplying.
God did not give Israel's future kings a numerical allowance of 700 wives, or 70, or even seven.
He prohibited the royal practice of multiplying wives.
The command did not establish a specific numerical threshold. But it unmistakably condemned the accumulation of wives by a king.
And the reason was written into the same verse.
וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ — velo yasur levavo.
“So that his heart does not turn aside.”
God was not merely regulating the size of a royal household.
He was warning about the direction of a human heart.
The word levavo refers to his heart, the inner center of thought, desire, loyalty, and decision.
God knew that what a king gathered around himself could eventually compete for what belonged to God alone.
And the warning did not stop with marriage.
Deuteronomy 17 also prohibited the king from multiplying horses and greatly multiplying silver and gold.
Military power. Wealth. Wives.
Three areas in which an ancient king might seek security, status, pleasure, or political influence.
Three areas where a ruler could begin trusting what he possessed more than the God who established him.
Now consider what Scripture tells us about Solomon.
He accumulated horses and chariots (1 Kings 10:26–29).
He received extraordinary quantities of gold (1 Kings 10:14–25).
And then came the royal household.
First Kings 11:3 records:
“And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.” (KJV)
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
One thousand women in the royal household.
And one heart that belonged wholly to God only when it was surrendered to Him.
We should be careful here.

The Bible does not tell us that every marriage occurred for the same reason. Some royal marriages in the ancient world were connected with diplomatic alliances, and Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter illustrates such a connection (1 Kings 3:1).
Nor does Scripture describe every woman in Solomon's household as personally responsible for his sin.
Solomon was the king.
He made choices.
He bore responsibility.
The women were not the excuse for his disobedience.

And the foreign women specifically mentioned in 1 Kings 11 were connected to another divine prohibition: Israel was not to enter marriages that would draw the people into the worship of other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4; 1 Kings 11:1–2).
That means Solomon's situation involved overlapping failures.
The multiplication of wives violated the royal instruction of Deuteronomy 17:17.
His attachment to women associated with forbidden religious alliances also disregarded God's warnings against idolatry.
And his eventual participation in false worship exposed where those compromises had led.
But there is something else in Deuteronomy 17 that makes this story even more heartbreaking.
God had commanded that when an Israelite king sat upon the throne, he was to write for himself a copy of the law, under the supervision of the Levitical priests, and read it throughout his life.
Why?
“So that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them.” (Deuteronomy 17:19, ESV)
The king was not supposed to stand above God's Word.
He was supposed to live beneath its authority.
His throne did not exempt him.
His wisdom did not exempt him.
His wealth did not exempt him.
His calling did not exempt him.
And neither does ours.
Scripture does not tell us whether Solomon personally completed the commanded royal copy of the law. We should not invent that detail.
But we can say this with certainty: the command was there, and the king was accountable to it.
Now imagine the weight of that truth.
A man could build the temple and still disobey the God worshiped within it.
He could offer sacrifices and still protect desires God had forbidden.
He could possess wisdom and still fail to practice it.
And that should disturb us more than the number 700.
Because most of us will never sit on a throne.
Most of us will never command armies, receive tribute from nations, or build a temple covered in gold.
But we know what it means to make exceptions.
We know what it feels like to recognize a command of God and quietly search for a reason it might not apply to us.
We know how easily the heart can say, “Just this once.”
Or, “God understands.”
Or, “At least I am not doing what other people are doing.”
Or perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
“I can handle it.”
Solomon's story confronts that confidence.
Not because every questionable decision immediately becomes open rebellion.
Not because every hardship is punishment for some hidden sin.
But because persistent, defended disobedience can reshape the affections of a person who once seemed deeply devoted to God.
And Scripture gives us no permission to believe that spiritual maturity makes us immune.
In fact, Solomon's beginning makes his ending especially devastating.
When the Lord appeared to him at Gibeon, Solomon did not initially ask for long life, riches, or the death of his enemies.
He asked for an understanding heart to govern God's people (1 Kings 3:5–12).
He recognized his inadequacy.
He knew the responsibility was greater than his natural ability.
And God was pleased with his request.
There was humility there.
Dependence.
A desire to judge rightly.
Solomon received extraordinary wisdom from God.
First Kings 4:29 describes the breadth of that gift.
But wisdom was never meant to replace obedience.
Knowledge of God's will is not the same thing as submission to God's will.
A person may understand the danger of pride while secretly feeding it.
A person may preach about forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
A person may quote Scripture against lust while protecting private habits that nourish it.
A person may sing about surrender while withholding the very thing God is confronting.
And a person may be gifted in ministry while neglecting the quiet obedience that keeps the soul humble.
That is why this story is not simply about ancient polygamy.
It is about the terrible possibility of becoming skilled at explaining truth while growing careless about living it.
Solomon's wisdom was real.
His disobedience was real.
Both truths belong in the story.
And if that makes you uncomfortable, perhaps it should.
Because the question is no longer merely, “How could Solomon have 700 wives?”
It becomes, “What have I allowed to multiply in my life that God has already warned me about?”
A habit?
An appetite?
An ambition?
A secret relationship?
A bitterness you have rehearsed so often that it now feels justified?
A craving for approval that has quietly become more important than faithfulness?
Maybe nobody sees it.
Maybe everyone still thinks you are doing well.
Maybe you still attend church, read Scripture, pray, serve, give, and encourage others.
Those things can be genuine expressions of faith.
But none of them makes cherished disobedience harmless.
And Solomon's palace reminds us that outward splendor can coexist with inward spiritual danger.
Then the account reaches one of its saddest sentences.

“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.” (1 Kings 11:4, KJV)
When Solomon was old.
Those words carry a particular sorrow.
A man who began with a prayer for wisdom reached old age with a divided heart.
We are not told the precise moment when each compromise began, nor can we reconstruct every private decision along the way.
But the biblical narrative shows a devastating progression from prohibited accumulation to misplaced affection and finally to idolatrous worship.
The Hebrew description of his heart is important.
וְלֹא־הָיָה לְבָבוֹ שָׁלֵם עִם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהָיו
Velo hayah levavo shalem im-YHWH Elohav.
“And his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God.”
The word shalem (שָׁלֵם) conveys wholeness or completeness.
In this context, the issue was undivided covenant loyalty.
Solomon's heart was no longer wholly devoted to the Lord.
He had not simply made a poor administrative decision.
His worship had become compromised.
First Kings 11:5–8 names the gods and practices associated with his apostasy, including Ashtoreth, Milcom, Chemosh, and Molech.
Solomon even built high places connected with the worship of foreign deities.
The man who built a temple for the name of the Lord also built places associated with gods the Lord had forbidden His people to worship.
Can you feel the weight of that contradiction?
The same reign.
The same king.
The same life.
A temple dedicated to the living God.
And high places dedicated to false gods.
That is what divided allegiance can eventually look like when sin is allowed to settle in and make itself at home.
And here is a truth we must not soften.
God did not approve of Solomon's conduct simply because Solomon remained powerful.
The prosperity of a person is not proof that every part of that person's life pleases God.
A successful ministry is not proof that its leader has no need of repentance.
An expanding platform is not proof of divine endorsement of every decision.
And the fact that consequences have not yet appeared does not mean the warning was unnecessary.
God's patience is not permission to disobey Him.
First Kings 11:9 tells us that the Lord was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
Twice.
Solomon had received extraordinary revelation.
Yet extraordinary spiritual experiences did not eliminate his responsibility to obey.
Then judgment came.
God announced that the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's house, though, for David's sake, the full rupture would not occur during Solomon's lifetime (1 Kings 11:11–13).
And after Solomon's death, the kingdom divided during the reign of his son Rehoboam (1 Kings 12).
The consequences reached beyond Solomon himself.
That should make every one of us consider the influence of our choices.
Not every private sin becomes a national crisis.
Not every failure carries the same earthly consequences.
But our decisions can affect people who never participated in making them.
A spouse.
A child.
A congregation.
A friend.
Someone who trusted our example.
Someone learning what it means to follow Jesus by watching how we live.
And perhaps this is where Solomon's story begins to hurt.
Because you may be reading this with a particular compromise already on your mind.
Not because someone has named it.
Not because I know your private life.
But because the Holy Spirit uses the Word of God to expose what we would rather keep hidden.
Hebrews 4:12 describes God's Word as living and active, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
And when Scripture exposes us, the right response is not to defend ourselves.
It is to come into the light.
Perhaps you have spent years telling yourself that your spiritual life is fine because you still believe the right things.
But belief is not meant to remain a collection of correct statements disconnected from obedience.
Jesus asked in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” (KJV)
That question is not comfortable.
It was never intended to be.
And yet there is mercy in being confronted before our hearts become harder.
There is mercy in a warning that interrupts us.
There is mercy in the conviction that says, “This cannot continue.”
Because God does not expose sin merely to leave sinners in despair.
He calls us to repentance.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what we have done.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction that involves turning from sin toward God.
It is not a performance designed to purchase forgiveness.
It is the fitting response of a heart brought to recognize its sin before a holy and merciful God.
And that brings us to the most important part of Solomon's story.
Not the 700 wives.
Not the 300 concubines.
Not the gold.
Not even the divided kingdom.
The most important part is the greater King to whom the whole biblical story ultimately points.
Jesus Christ.
Because Solomon was wise, but he was not sinless.
Solomon was a son of David, but he was not the final promised Son of David.
Solomon built a magnificent temple, but he could not save the human heart from sin.
And the very Scriptures that record his glory also preserve the record of his failure.
Then, centuries later, Jesus stood before people who admired Solomon's greatness and said:
“And, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” (Matthew 12:42, KJV)
A greater than Solomon.
The Greek reads:
πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε
Pleion Solomōnos hōde.
“Something greater than Solomon is here.”
In the context of Matthew 12:42, Jesus was confronting people who failed to respond rightly to the wisdom and authority present in Him.
He was not merely claiming to be another impressive teacher.
He was declaring a greatness surpassing Solomon.
And the contrast becomes astonishing when we consider their lives.
Solomon received wisdom.
Christ is the One in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).
Solomon's heart turned away.
Christ remained obedient to the Father, even unto death (Philippians 2:8).
Solomon's disobedience contributed to the tearing of a kingdom.
Christ, through His blood, brings those who were far off near to God and makes peace (Ephesians 2:13–16).
Solomon's glory could not rescue him from the consequences of sin.
Christ's glory was revealed through a cross where He bore sin to bring sinners to God (1 Peter 3:18).
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a beautiful religious idea.
Because perhaps your story is not one of faithfulness from beginning to end.
Perhaps you have made promises to God that you later broke.
Perhaps you have known Scripture for years and still fallen into sins you once condemned.
Perhaps you have been the person everyone thought was strong while privately wondering how you became so spiritually exhausted.
Perhaps you have prayed, “Lord, how did I get here?”
And perhaps the shame has convinced you that your failure must be the final chapter.
But listen carefully.
The Bible does not tell us that Solomon's late-life repentance is certain.

Ecclesiastes is traditionally associated with Solomon, and some readers understand it as reflecting a later recognition of the emptiness of life pursued apart from God. But Scripture does not explicitly narrate Solomon's final repentance, so we must not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
We do not need to invent a happy ending for Solomon to proclaim the genuine hope available in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is already sufficient.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired our reputation.
Not after every consequence disappeared.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy of another opportunity.
Christ died for sinners.
And 1 John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to treat sin casually.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
To confess.
To turn.
To trust the finished work of Jesus Christ.
To receive mercy without pretending that what we did was harmless.
Because grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings us into the light and teaches us to walk there.
Titus 2:11–12 tells us that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
And grace transforms.
It is not permission to keep building the altars that are destroying us.
It is God's kindness calling us to tear them down.
Maybe that is the word you needed today.
Not another reminder that you have failed.
You already know where you have failed.
Maybe what you need is the courage to stop negotiating with what God has already called sin.
To end the relationship that is drawing you away from Christ.
To confess the dishonesty.
To seek help for the addiction.
To release the bitterness.
To abandon the hidden habit.
To apologize without excuses.
To return to prayer, not as a performance, but as a child coming home to the Father.

And if your struggle is complicated, if you have been wounded, coerced, or harmed by someone else's sin, please do not mistake this call to repentance for a command to accept abuse or carry responsibility for another person's wrongdoing.
God's truth does not require you to remain in danger.
Coming into the light can include seeking safety, wise pastoral care, professional help, and support from trustworthy people.
Real discipleship does not demand that you pretend everything is fine.
It calls you toward truth.
And the truth is that Jesus is not impressed by the palace we have built to conceal the condition of our hearts.
He sees what is real.
He knows what we have done.
And He is mighty to save those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So here is the question that has been waiting beneath Solomon's story all along.
If God has already spoken about something in your life, what are you still trying to justify?
You do not have to answer publicly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your wounds or sins.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And perhaps your first prayer tonight can be as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have defended things You have called me to surrender. I have sometimes loved Your blessings more than Your will. Forgive me. Search my heart. Teach me to obey You, not merely speak about You. Give me the courage to leave what is drawing me away. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
You can simply write “No more hiding” if you are choosing honesty before God.
Or “Pray for me” if you are struggling and need your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you.

And if God has carried you through a season of compromise into repentance and restoration, consider sharing a testimony. Your story may encourage someone who believes they are beyond the reach of mercy.
You do not need to disclose anything that would compromise your safety or privacy.
Sometimes even a few honest words can remind another believer that they are not fighting alone.
And please, do not let this message end with you if someone else might need its biblical warning and Gospel hope.
Send it privately to someone who has been asking difficult questions about the Bible.
Because we do not want people merely to admire powerful words.
We want people to encounter the truth of God's Word and be pointed faithfully to Jesus Christ.
There is also a way to help sustain and expand this work.
It does not purchase grace, forgiveness, answered prayer, or a greater place in His kingdom.
And it should never replace the financial responsibilities you already have toward your family, your local church, or those in need.

Biblically, the Old Testament tithe had a particular role in Israel's covenant life, while the New Testament teaches believers to give willingly, generously, and without compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Those products are not the heart of this ministry.
Jesus is.
Our desire is that believers become more rooted in Scripture, more discerning in truth, more humble in repentance, and more steadfast in following Christ.
Please give only as you are able and willing, never under pressure or guilt.
But your willing partnership can help make more biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
And even if you cannot give financially, your prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share Gospel-centered content are deeply meaningful ways to participate.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to Solomon.
The king who asked for wisdom.
The king who built the temple.
The king whose wealth astonished nations.
The king who multiplied wives despite a warning already written in God's law.
The king whose heart was eventually turned toward other gods.
Do you see the warning?
It was never enough to have a magnificent beginning.
Solomon needed a faithful heart.
And so do we.
Jesus said, “If ye love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15, KJV).
Not because obedience earns salvation.
But because love for Christ is not meant to remain an empty confession.
And when we fail, our hope is not that our record was somehow better than Solomon's.
Our hope is Jesus Christ, who died for our sins, rose again, and calls us to Himself.
That is the heart of From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not minimizing the damage of sin.
Not promising that every earthly consequence will disappear.
But proclaiming that through Jesus Christ, guilty sinners can receive forgiveness, broken lives can be transformed, and those who have wandered can turn back to the living God.
Solomon's story warns us not to presume upon wisdom, privilege, spiritual experiences, or past obedience.
The Gospel calls us to trust the One who is greater than Solomon.
And if you remember nothing else from this article, remember this:
The most dangerous thing Solomon multiplied was not merely the number of wives in his palace, but the compromises he allowed to compete for his heart.
So do not wait until the consequences become visible before taking God's warnings seriously.
Come to Christ today.
Not with a polished reputation.
Not with a list of excuses.
But with the truth.
Because the King who is greater than Solomon is still calling sinners to repentance, and everyone who comes to Him in faith will find that His mercy is greater than the sin they could never undo.
Solomon had a thousand women in his royal household, but the question that follows us home is whether Jesus has our whole heart.
